title: csv.writer writes rows in list form to a CSV file
body: `csv.writer` takes a row as an ordered set of values—such as a list or tuple—and writes it to a CSV file. `writerow()` is a method for writing a single row, and it eliminates the need to manually handle commas between values.
detail: If you concatenate a CSV directly as a string, it can be confusing to handle commas, quotes, and line breaks. Using `csv.writer` allows you to safely write each value one character at a time. When opening a file, you typically specify both `newline=''` and `encoding='utf-8'`. Beginners should understand that they first write the header row using `writerow`, and then add the data rows in the same way.

title: csv.DictWriter uses the keys of the dictionary as column names.
body: csv.DictWriter is used to save dictionary data as a CSV file. fieldnames specifies the column names and their order, and writeheader() writes the header row.
detail: If the row data is a dictionary, you can save it using `writerow(row)`. In this case, the dictionary keys must match the field names for the values to be written to the correct columns. When saving multiple rows, first write the column names using `writeheader()`, and then write each row using `writerow()`.

title: The results from `DictReader` can be read like a dictionary, row by row.
body: csv.DictReader reads each row as a dictionary, using the CSV headers as keys. Using `list(reader)` allows you to collect multiple rows into a list.
detail: When reading a CSV file and then filtering or transforming the data, it’s common to collect the rows into a list for processing. While `rows = list(reader)` loads all rows into memory—which is convenient for training with small files—it’s also important to get into the habit of processing large files one row at a time using `for row in reader`.

title: Typos in CSV column names are a common cause of KeyErrors.
body: Inspect reader.fieldnames and explicitly validate required columns at startup. row.get('score') can be useful for an optional column, but it can silently turn a missing required score into None. If headers are normalized, preserve the original names and document the rule.
